content: 1. Sugammadex Sodium: Sugammadex may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives (containing estrogen or progestogen) by competing for receptor binding. A bolus dose of sugammadex is equivalent to missing one or more doses of hormonal contraceptives. Patients using oral, transdermal, or implantable hormonal contraceptives on the same day as sugammadex should use an additional non-hormonal contraceptive method (e.g., condoms with spermicide) for the next 7 days. 2. Tipranavir: This drug can significantly alter estrogen plasma levels, potentially reducing the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended during co-administration. 3. Tovorafenib: Tovorafenib, a weak CYP3A4 inducer, decreases the levels of levonorgestrel and ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic and intestinal metabolism. Avoid co-administration with hormonal contraceptives. If unavoidable, use an additional non-hormonal contraceptive method during treatment and for 28 days after discontinuation. 4. Topiramate: Topiramate reduces the levels of ethinyl estradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially decreasing contraceptive efficacy. Non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 5. Tucatinib: Tucatinib increases the levels of ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration with CYP3A substrates where small concentration changes may lead to serious toxicities. If unavoidable, reduce the dose of the CYP3A substrate as per product labeling. 6. Albiglutide: Ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel may reduce the hypoglycemic effects of antidiabetic drugs like albiglutide by impairing glucose tolerance. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 7. Amoxicillin and Other Antibiotics: Antibiotics like amoxicillin, ampicillin, and cephalosporins (e.g., cefaclor, cefadroxil) may reduce the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives by altering intestinal flora. Although the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 8. Carbamazepine: This drug decreases the levels of levonorgestrel and ethinyl estradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing contraceptive efficacy. Additional contraceptive methods are recommended. 9. Clobazam: Clobazam, a weak CYP3A4 inducer, may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended during co-administration. 10. Cimetidine: Cimetidine increases the levels of ethinyl estradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for potential adverse effects. 11. Dexamethasone: Dexamethasone decreases the levels of levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for reduced contraceptive efficacy. 12. Darunavir: Darunavir may significantly alter estrogen plasma levels, potentially reducing the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 13. Elagolix: Elagolix, a weak-to-moderate CYP3A4 inducer, reduces the levels of ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel. Monitor CYP3A substrates and consider increasing their dose if needed. 14. Fluconazole: Fluconazole increases the levels of ethinyl estradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for potential adverse effects. 15. Grapefruit: Grapefruit increases the levels of ethinyl estradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for potential adverse effects. 16. Griseofulvin: Griseofulvin decreases the levels of levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Additional contraceptive methods are recommended. 17. Insulin and Antidiabetics: Ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel may reduce the hypoglycemic effects of insulin and other antidiabetic drugs by impairing glucose tolerance. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 18. Iloperidone: Iloperidone increases the levels of ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for potential adverse effects. 19. Fostemsavir: Fostemsavir inhibits BCRP transporters, potentially increasing the levels of ethinyl estradiol. Avoid co-administration or adjust the dose of BCRP substrates. 20. Elafibranor: Switch to effective non-hormonal contraceptives or add a barrier method during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose. 21. Etravirine: Etravirine decreases the levels of ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Additional contraceptive methods are recommended. 22. Exenatide: Exenatide may reduce the absorption of oral contraceptives by slowing gastric emptying. Advise patients to take oral contraceptives at least 1 hour before exenatide administration. 23. Felbamate: Felbamate decreases the levels of levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for reduced contraceptive efficacy. 24. Flibanserin: Ethinyl estradiol increases the levels of flibanserin by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for increased adverse effects. 25. Fosphenytoin: Fosphenytoin decreases the levels of levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for reduced contraceptive efficacy. 26. Gemifloxacin: Gemifloxacin may reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives by altering intestinal flora. Although the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 27. Green Tea: Ethinyl estradiol increases the levels of green tea by reducing its elimination. Monitor for potential adverse effects. 28. Hemins: Ethinyl estradiol may reduce the effects of hemins by increasing delta-aminolevulinic acid synthetase. Monitor for reduced efficacy. 29. Hylauronidase: Estrogens may render tissues partially resistant to hyaluronidase, requiring larger doses for equivalent effects. 30. Encorafenib: Encorafenib inhibits and induces CYP3A4, potentially altering the efficacy and toxicity of hormonal contraceptives. Monitor closely and adjust doses as needed. 31. Cobicistat: Cobicistat increases the levels of ethinyl estradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration with CYP3A4 substrates associated with serious toxicities. 32. Darunavir: Darunavir decreases the levels of ethinyl estradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 33. Dabrafenib: Dabrafenib decreases the levels of ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for reduced contraceptive efficacy. 34. Danicopan: Danicopan increases the levels of ethinyl estradiol by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Dose adjustments may be necessary. 35. Erythromycin: Erythromycin may reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives by altering intestinal flora. Although the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 36. Efavirenz: Efavirenz decreases the levels of levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for reduced contraceptive efficacy. 37. Fineronone: Ethinyl estradiol increases the levels of fineronone by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor serum potassium and adjust doses as needed. 38. Fluvoxamine: Ethinyl estradiol increases the levels of fluvoxamine by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Monitor for potential adverse effects. 39. Insulin Glargine: Ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel may reduce the hypoglycemic effects of insulin glargine by impairing glucose tolerance. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 40. Iloperidone: Iloperidone increases the levels of ethinyl estradiol and levonorgestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for potential adverse effects. This list highlights the importance of monitoring and adjusting therapy when hormonal contraceptives are co-administered with other medications.
